arms.note: Both arms run the identical local model on identical prompts, so model size is held constant and only harness behaviour varies. Critics receive the two run directories with no arm labels. This measures whether a round improved the app; it does not measure the app against a reference product.

rounds.label: Setup
rounds.what: Baseline pinned, six dimensions audited against real code, capture harness and 18-task shared set built.
rounds.findings: 88 evidence-backed gaps, 28 of them high severity, every one carrying a file:line or an executed probe.

rounds.label: Six dimensions, one gap each
rounds.what: Six builders in isolated worktrees, one dimension each, every fix carrying a new mechanical case. Two semantic merge conflicts resolved by composing both designs rather than picking one.
rounds.findings: Two losses, both real. V3 above. VC3: the contrast fix never reached the chrome — both arms render identical ink at 2.45:1, and the round-1 build lost only for having MORE text in it, including its own “nothing was computed” caution at 2.46:1. Behind that sits the round’s worst finding: test/styleCheck.ts passes at ≥4.5:1 while inspecting the --text-* tokens, and the app’s chrome uses 242 raw text-neutral-* classes the check never looks at. A green check was certifying a property the app does not have.
rounds.verdict: Round-1 build 6 · baseline 2 · 9 ties, over 17 tasks judged blind by 17 fresh-context critics reading the real runs.
rounds.gap: V3: the new verification chrome manufactures confidence it has not earned. On a question the library does not cover, the round-1 build showed a passed recomputation, a “the checker compared the reply against that output” line and a revision claiming unsupported items were removed — while re-deriving its numbers from constants the model invented and labelling one “EPA standard estimate” with no source consulted. The baseline simply said the library does not cover home repair, so this is general knowledge. Looking checked beat being checked, which is the one thing this project exists to prevent.
rounds.fix: Retrieval arms the measurement check · tool claims joined to the executed set · failed tools stop disarming the link checks · plan-step tool calls made visible · action row follows the answer, waits get names · streamed error frames diagnosed and recoverable · long tokens wrap, focus rings restored, prose contrast raised

rounds.label: Send the losses back

pair.A: the original baseline — the build that beat us in round 1

rounds.what: Five builders: the two losses, plus the three ties where BOTH arms failed the reader — a cancelled plan with no cancelled state, a Stop rendered as a step failure, and an empty review reported as a clean review.
rounds.findings: V3, the round-1 loss, is now won at high confidence: the build says “Recomputation ran, but its inputs are constants the model wrote… Treat these figures as unverified” and “Nothing in the library covers this question — the answer is not backed by it”, where the baseline printed a “📖 From the library:” strip with five ranked passages under an answer about faucets. VC3 flipped too, measured off the pixels: the provenance line went 2.46:1 → 9.48:1, the timing readout 2.48:1 → 5.26:1, and text below AA in the last reply went 11 of 20 → 0 of 20.
rounds.verdict: Round-2 build 13 · baseline 1 · 2 ties, over 16 tasks judged blind (a 17th critic failed on schema retries and is not counted). Both round-1 losses flipped to wins at high confidence.
rounds.gap: TH3, tool-honesty: quotation fidelity. Neither build compares a quoted span in the reply against the retrieved passage it claims to quote — the baseline won this one on the model’s luck, not on anything the app did. The critic ran the exact substring test in ten lines of Python against data the app already holds in the same message.
rounds.fix: Circular recomputation reports the weaker state · a retrieval turn with no relevant passages says so instead of showing a provenance strip · plans get a real terminal state · a user’s Stop is not drawn as a step failure · an empty review is disclosed instead of reported as a clean one · citation markers are numbered and their locators reachable · chrome contrast measured against the surfaces it is composited over

rounds.label: The tool-honesty family, and the residuals
rounds.what: Five builders: quotation fidelity and tool-use claims (the round-2 loss), markdown wrap plus a palette-level retint, a verification pass that could not succeed, stall self-detection, and three plan residuals.
rounds.findings: The quote checker fired exactly as intended on TH1 — “⚠️ Quoted as exact but in no tool output this turn” naming the invented span and the tool it checked against — and correctly stayed silent on TH3, where both replies quoted accurately. FR2 now counts the silence out loud: “still waiting on the model · 1:30 · gives up at 5:00”, where the baseline’s 60s and 90s frames are byte-identical. VC3 went from 9 failing text nodes to 0, floor 2.46:1 → 5.21:1.
rounds.verdict: Round-3 build 13 · baseline 0 · 2 ties · 1 VOID, over 16 tasks. Corrected downward from 14–0–2: the baseline arm had been handicapped (see round 4), which voids TTU2 and weakens V3.
rounds.gap: Two, both in the winning build. The quote checker FALSE-POSITIVED on V2, flagging a quotation that is verbatim in the reference_lookup output it names — a verifier that cries wolf teaches the reader to ignore it, which costs more than the numbering gains. And on TTU2 the app stamps a green ✓ and “it runs without error” over a reply whose stated sum (854,405) contradicts its own executed output (824,693): the check verifies that no exception was raised, not that the numbers match, so the reassurance fires hardest exactly where the answer is wrong.
rounds.fix: Quoted spans checked character-for-character against captured tool output · citation attributions checked against the passage the marker resolves to · a “Tools used” section that names none of the executed calls is contradicted · assistant markdown wraps and code blocks gain a wrap toggle · the raw-neutral guard widened to the whole renderer · a silent stream counts itself out loud and names its deadline · plans disclose what each step may DO before approval · a terminal outcome is the heaviest text in the block · never-run steps stop presenting their contents as findings

rounds.label: Four reassurances the app had not earned

pair.A: the original baseline, this time WITH the Python runtime it had been missing

rounds.what: Five builders on the two faults blind critics found in round 3’s winner, the tie where a check still could not succeed, a cold boot attributed nowhere, and a plan forecast nothing verified — plus the harness guard that let a handicapped arm score for three rounds.
rounds.findings: The quote checker’s false positive is gone and its true positive survives: on TH1 it now names both an undisclosed tool and an invented quotation, and a critic confirmed neither warning is spurious. The claim check stops at the first unreachable source — 7 searches down to 2, post-answer lockout 21.3 s down to 1.4 s, a 15× difference against the same dead provider. The cold sandbox boot is named and quantified — “started the sandbox in 1.6 s, then failed after 7 ms” — where the baseline still reports a cold call as 8 ms against a warm 20 ms.
rounds.verdict: Round-4 build 13 · baseline 3 · 1 tie, over 17 tasks judged blind against a corrected baseline. More losses than round 3 reported — because round 3 was judged against a handicapped arm and this was not.
rounds.gap: Three losses, and the honest reading differs per task. V3: our run hit the 300 s capture budget mid-verification and a critic judged an unfinished turn; re-captured it finishes at 268 s against the baseline’s 213 s, so we are slower and the tail is still unexplained, but the “never finished” reasoning was partly a capture artifact. V1: our build stated 165°F / 74°C, which appear in none of the retrieved passages, and printed “✎ Revised: 1 unsupported item were sent back for verification or removal” — a claim of resolution that did not occur. That is the same false-assurance species this round set out to kill, in a new place. TH2: the baseline won on a provenance line ours did not print.
rounds.fix: Bracketed citation markers trimmed before a quoted span is checked · printed figures compared against the figures the reply states · the unreachable-source rule inverted so an unlisted error code cannot defeat it · the sandbox boot measured, named and reported beside the run time · a plan step reconciled against the tools it actually ran · validity extended twice: a precondition that did not hold, and a turn that never ended

rounds.label: The shape three rounds of checks kept failing in

pair.A: the original baseline, with the Python runtime

rounds.what: Five builders: the revision line that claimed work it had not done, the measurement check that missed the case it was built for, the unbounded verification tail, a memory disclosure the current build had lost, and citation markers that resolved to the wrong passage when a turn ran two lookups.
rounds.findings: The round produced a finding larger than its fixes. Three rounds running, a check built for exactly the failing case did not fire, always for the same structural reason: it enumerated the forms it had already seen and the world supplied one that was not on the list — round 3 listed net:: error codes and missed ERR_UNSAFE_PORT; round 4 bounded a quoted span by the line so a citation marker inside it broke the match; round 5 armed measurements per unit STRING, so a corpus with no Celsius never checked 74°C at all, and 165°F was named only because one passage incidentally mentioned a fridge at 40°F. Round 3’s repair generalises: replace the enumeration with its inverse — list the few codes that mean a server ANSWERED and treat everything else as unreachable. A list of known-bad can be defeated by an unknown; a list of known-good cannot.
rounds.verdict: Round-5 build 15 · baseline 1 · 1 tie, over 17 tasks judged blind. Best result so far, and the single loss has one traceable cause that was documented as open before judging began.
rounds.gap: V1, the one loss, and the cause was known before judging. The app now catches and NAMES the invented figure — “✎ Revised: 1 unsupported item was sent back (165 °F)” — but the re-check then clears it, and the figure is still in the answer. reviseAgainstFindings passes the turn’s records into the agent loop, so a retrieval made DURING the correction joins the corpus the re-check reads, while onToolExecuted writes only the audit log and never patches toolCalls. The food-safety pack does contain “165°F (74°C)”, so a real passage cleared both figures — one the reader never saw. The app is not lying about the re-check; the re-check is reading evidence the reader has no access to.
rounds.fix: The revision line is a function of the report before AND after, names the surviving items, and is amber rather than green when a finding stands · temperature became one dimension in two scales, and stopped being derivable, since the integer-multiple rule had been certifying 80°F from a fridge’s 40°F · the tail is bounded at 60s with a named expiry and the stat line now reads “25.7s answer · 54.3s checking · 80.0s total” · a source tool that found nothing says so, on the block header and to the badge · passages are numbered per turn, so a second lookup no longer restarts at [1] under a reply that cites across both

rounds.label: The re-check that reads what the reader cannot

pair.A: the original baseline, with the Python runtime

rounds.what: Four builders on round 5’s only loss and the residue around it: the correction pass that cleared a finding using a retrieval the reader never saw; the pre-model wait billed to the wrong phase; a contact check that cried wolf on a base64 token while a $34,000 figure walked past the gate; and three tool outcomes — never sent, server failed, returned nothing — that all rendered as one indistinguishable ✗.
rounds.findings: The headline is a number the app cannot see. Measured against the harness’s own wall clock, the baseline’s stat line was off by more than 25% on 7 of 17 turns, worst 3.08× — V2 claimed “32.4s total” on a turn that took 99.9 s. The round-6 build was off by more than 25% on 0 of 16, worst 1.01×, median 1.00; the residual tenth of a second is the harness’s own send-to-stamp offset. The cause was one line: turnStartedAt was stamped AFTER gatherTurnContext, so every pre-model search was billed to nobody. TTU1 shows it directly — the baseline reads “13.45s to first token · 31.5s total” on a turn the reader sat through for 40.3 s, while the round-6 build reads “12.80s to first token · 8.7s gathering · 31.1s answer · 39.7s total” against a measured 39.8 s.
rounds.verdict: Round-6 build 16 · baseline 0 · 1 tie, over 17 tasks judged blind. The best result of the six rounds, the first with no losses against the corrected baseline, and the sweep behind it was 17/17 VALID with 0 screenshot failures. The tie is honest rather than a wash: on TH1 neither model invented a tool claim, so neither app was put to the test.
rounds.gap: Six of the seventeen critiques land on the same species the project set out to kill, in places we had not looked. VC1: the app prints “Recomputed the stated figures in Python; the checker compared the reply against that output” under a reply whose echoed string plainly disagrees with the Python output inches below it — the checker compares FIGURES, the sentence claims it compared THE REPLY. PT1: we flag tools that ran without being forecast and never flag the reverse, so a plan that promised list_notes and read_note and ran neither says nothing while its header reads “4/4 steps done”. TH3: a quote warning fires on a span differing from the source only by curly-versus-straight quote glyphs, and the 60-character truncation stops before the deviation, so the reader sees a fabrication warning on a verbatim quote with no visible difference. TH1 (the tie): the reply misreports the ARGUMENT it passed — it states query "ground beef safe internal temperature" where the audit shows the whole user prompt went — and nothing checks a reply’s account of what it passed a tool. And the warning line itself is ungrammatical in every plural case, because the verb agrees with the number of CATEGORIES rather than the number of items.
rounds.fix: The correction pass publishes its tool calls, so a clearance can only rest on evidence that rendered — on V1 the same figure that round 5 cleared invisibly is now named and left standing, and 165 appears in zero retrieved passages · turnOpenedAt is stamped before gatherTurnContext, so the line reads “13.45s to first token · 8.8s gathering · 31.5s answer · 40.3s total” · never-sent, server-failed and returned-nothing became three states with the reason on the collapsed row (↩ declined: the query was a sentence about you, not search terms) and a “Tool calls 3 · 1 declined” count · the contact check stopped starting mid-token, and the figure gate stopped discarding what unsourcedFigures had already found

rounds.label: Five checks that read the quantity next to the one they meant

pair.A: the original baseline, re-captured through the current harness

rounds.what: Five builders on round 6’s critiques: the recompute sentence that claimed more than it measured, the plan forecast checked in one direction only, the quote warning whose truncation hid the difference it was warning about, a reply’s unchecked account of its own tool ARGUMENTS, and the instrument gap that made a rendering bug undiagnosable.
rounds.findings: The round’s largest finding is a bug in the shipped renderer that six rounds of critics could not see, because they were reading the renderer’s own output. Adding reply.md — the raw markdown, beside the rendered text — exposed two independent character-eating defects with the same consequence. latexToPlainText was pairing dollar sigils into a math span and deleting the prose between them: “Cash or traveler’s checks ($200–$500 minimum)” reached the reader as “(200–500 minimum)”. And marked’s GFM single-tilde strikethrough was pairing approximations: “~51 GPH (~0.9 GPM)” reached the reader as “51 GPH (0.9 GPM)” — an estimate turned into an exact figure in the line a reader is most likely to quote. The grounding warning naming $0.01, $36, $10 had been RIGHT every time it fired, and was read as a cry-wolf because the figures genuinely were not on screen. When a check and the screen disagree, the screen is a measurement too, and it can be the broken one.
rounds.verdict: Round-7 build 18 · baseline 0 · 0 ties, over 18 tasks — the full set for the first time, since VC2 had never had a baseline capture to pair against. Both sweeps 18/18 VALID, 0 failed. Read the caveat before the number: this is the widest margin of the seven rounds AND the round whose judging was most biased toward it.
rounds.gap: The 18–0 is inflated and the reason is mine. This round’s critic prompts named the specific checks the round had just built — “compare the forecast IN BOTH DIRECTIONS”, “does the collapsed row say why”, “measure the pixels, not the declared colour”. A critic told to measure the thing we optimised will find that we win. Earlier rounds’ prompts stayed closer to each task’s own `probes` field; round 7’s drifted toward the changelog, so this score is not comparable with rounds 1–6 and must not be read as a trend. Round 8 must derive critic prompts from tasks.json alone, written by someone who has not seen what changed. Separately: the baseline is seven rounds old, so a sweep against it measures accumulated distance, not this round’s work. And the critics still found real defects in every winning run, several of them self-inflicted — the VC1 layout fix set `overflow-wrap: anywhere` on all markdown, which now breaks the word “Passage” across three lines as “Pas/sag/e” in a table header sized to a `[1]` cell.
rounds.fix: The recompute notice narrowed to what it measures, and the string gap it can no longer claim is recorded as open · the plan reconciliation returns the whole symmetric difference, so a forecast tool that never ran is named · quote warnings show a window centred on the divergence with ⟪⟫ marking the break, replacing a clamp that cut BEFORE the differing character and printed byte-identical text for an honest quotation and a falsified one · a new rung checks a reply’s account of its own arguments · the verb agrees with the number of items rather than the number of categories · the amber banner’s confession line 3.10:1 → 6.66:1, after the contrast suite was found reading getComputedStyle().color, which opacity does not touch · scripts/test.sh typechecks the project instead of a hand-listed 66 files · make-blind-pairs scrubs the app root and then VERIFIES the blinding, after TTU2 was found shipping the baseline’s own directory name inside run.json

rounds.label: Judging that is not written by the person being judged
rounds.what: Five builders on defects blind critics found in runs the app WON in round 7 — three of them caused by this project’s own earlier fixes — plus the first attempt to remove the judge’s conflict of interest.
rounds.findings: The method was the round’s real subject, and the agent sent to write neutral prompts came back with a worse problem than the one it was sent to fix: all 18 `probes` fields in tasks.json are defect descriptions of a specific build, and four of them quote constants only one build can produce — VC3’s "roughly 2.05:1 … 33 places … 83 places", VC2’s "33 occurrences of outline-none", PT2’s exact button strings, PT3’s glyphs and classes. A critic that measures 2.46:1 against 9.48:1 having read that the number to beat is 2.05:1 is recognising an arm, not judging one. That was true of every round before this one. Critics now read a generated view carrying only id, dimension, prompt and setup, and the generator refuses to write if a stripped field survives under any name. A second guard came out of the version question: the sidebar renders the app version, so it is in every screenshot and cannot be scrubbed — eight rounds of blind judging worked only because package.json had never been bumped. Staging now refuses a pair whose arms report different versions.
rounds.verdict: Round-8 build 2 · round-7 build 0 · 16 ties, over 18 tasks. Read alongside round 7’s 18–0–0, this is the number that means something: it is the first round compared against the PREVIOUS round rather than a seven-round-old baseline, judged with prompts written by an agent that never saw the changelog, from a task file stripped of the fields that name known defects. Sixteen ties is the correct answer when two builds one round apart are the same program on sixteen of eighteen tasks.
rounds.gap: The ties are informative in three different ways and they should not be read as one thing. Some are the tasks not being sensitive to what changed — no builder touched PT2, PT3, FR2 or FR3, and the critics correctly found the two runs byte-identical apart from timestamps. Some are the model not exercising the change: on V1 the round-7 arm fired a false positive on a figure its own tool output contained, and the critic refused to score it because the round-8 arm never received a multi-lookup turn — "its 0-mismatch score is untested rather than earned". And one is a gap in the task set: builder A’s fix is visible in the artifacts — round 7 prints "the answer is not backed by it" while marking two passages cited, round 8 prints "the answer cites [3] [5] from it anyway" — but TH3’s neutral question asks whether source text is checkable on screen, which both builds satisfy, so a real repair to a self-contradiction scored a tie. The task set measures the dimension, not the defect.
rounds.fix: Citation markers resolve across every lookup, not just the first, and "— not cited" is only asserted when the binder could resolve the marker · the currency pattern reads the whole number, so $0.007 is no longer reported as $0.00, and the ladder arms by dimension with two of its three bounds set by cry-wolf the suite caught · overflow-wrap: anywhere replaced by break-word plus a scroll container, ending 6 shredded words per reply while keeping the 220-character token inside the column · a failure boundary that gives the reader a sentence and keeps the identifier in the disclosure, the audit log and a copy affordance · the bench captures dark theme for the first time in eight rounds, and its keyboard traversal now activates a control and continues into what opens

rounds.label: Defects both builds share, found once the judging stopped flattering us
rounds.what: Five builders on defects a same-generation comparison exposed as shared by BOTH builds — the category rounds 1–7 could not see, because a seven-round-old baseline loses everything and the margin hides what neither side fixed.
rounds.findings: The wins were measured, not argued. VC2: obscured Tab stops 24–30 of 70 down to 0 of 70, identical in both themes and on both routes, with the focus indicator itself tying at 70/70 visible in every file — so the margin is occlusion alone. VC3: the SAME warning sentence at 3.11:1 in one build and 6.09:1 in the other, and the same failed-call line at 3.59:1 against 6.19:1, both below AA in light theme only — the defect a single raw palette step cannot avoid across two themes. V3: a coverage line naming what the pass never reached, which the critic credited to the application rather than the sampler because the older build’s extractor demonstrably handled the same ranges and printed nothing. That third win came from a builder that REFUSED the feature it was asked for, argued that ranking findings by importance would assert the app understood the question in the one place a reader cannot check it, and shipped a narrower true thing instead.
rounds.verdict: Round-9 build 3 · round-8 build 0 · 14 ties · 1 void, over 18 tasks. The second same-generation comparison, and the first judged with critic prompts generated MECHANICALLY from the task set — no agent and no person wrote them, so the contamination round 8’s prompt-writer disclosed about itself is structurally gone. The three wins map one-to-one onto three of the five builders; the two that scored ties were the code fold, which no task exercised, and the task set itself, which is the instrument rather than the subject.
rounds.gap: The void is V2, and voiding it was mine rather than the critic’s: the deciding event was one arm’s request overflowing the model’s 8192-token context on a turn where round 9 changed no context code, same prompt, same settings, same retrieval, single turn. The critic reached the same conclusion and said it lacked the evidence — "if that failure is environmental, this is a tie". A server condition is not the change under test. Precedent is round 3, which voided a task for the same reason. Separately, two round-9 improvements were visible in the artifacts and scored nothing, because neither was the task’s question: the older build draws one fact in two different amber ramps on one screen where round 9 uses a single token, and the older build lost the tail of an answer where round 9 did not. Builder E’s rewrite improved the questions and the tension it was sent to resolve is still there — a question neutral enough not to leak can still be blind to a real repair.
rounds.fix: Focus contained on all five covering surfaces by walking outward from the surface node, so a pane added anywhere is covered the day it is added · warning ink became tokens after the diagnosis changed from lightness to chroma — Tailwind ramps desaturate as they darken, so walking down the ramp buys contrast by spending the thing that means "warning" · a code fold that lands on a hyphen no longer also stops short of the edge, the pair that reads as hyphenation · the checker now says what it did NOT check, after the ranking it was asked for was judged unreliable and refused · all 18 probes rewritten on the principle that what leaks is not specificity but asserting a value

rounds.label: The turn says it is over while the answer is still arriving
rounds.what: Five builders on defects a same-generation comparison showed BOTH builds shared, plus the first scoring change since the bench began.
rounds.findings: The turn had been reporting itself over while the answer was still arriving — composer-idle was keyed on the last byte off the socket, not the last paint — and the still-arriving tail was painted at an opacity measured below AA on 71 of 73 frames at the real cadence, because the span is recreated on every paced flush. Not transient, as both a critic and I had assumed. A failed plan step announced itself to a screen reader with an accessible name byte-identical to a finished one, and so did running against pending; the plan-accessibility check that found it reported 9 failures on its own first draft against 128 on its second, because its locator was one of the things being located. And the app had been blaming the reader for a context budget it had mostly spent itself: of 6,508 tokens against an 8,192 window, 2,725 were the tool list the app adds and 2,048 the reply reservation, neither of them on the meter, which showed 1,735.
rounds.verdict: Round 10, scored in three columns that are reported side by side and never added: task — round-10 build 6 · round-9 build 1 · 11 ties. self-consistency — 2 · 2 · 14. record-consistency — 3 · 1 · 14. The columns earned their place immediately: "seen only by a cross-cutting column" is B 1 · A 1 — one fact for this build and one against it that a single verdict per task would have missed entirely.
rounds.gap: Two losses, and the first is the worse. V1: this build printed "⚠️ 1 measurement (165 °F) in this reply is not backed by the tool output" on a turn whose own retrieved passages state it seventeen times, including "| Chicken, turkey, and other poultry | … | 165°F (74°C) |". A false unverified on a poultry cooking temperature is the most damaging cry-wolf this app can produce. The distinguishing fact is that this arm ran THREE lookups and the other ran one, so the measurement corpus does not span every lookup in a turn — demonstrated in this build, untested in the other, which was never handed a multi-lookup turn. FR3: the expiry line reads "Ran: the code check. Not run: the recomputation." directly above the recomputation and its output; the round-9 build gets the same line right. Both were caught only because the task question tied and a cross-cutting column could still take a claim away.
rounds.fix: The composer waits for the last paint and the streaming tail floor moved to 0.66, first value clearing AA over the reply surface · every plan step state carries an accessible name and a dead row stops being a control · three checks stopped judging the wrong thing, including a quote checker that treated the credit line as part of the quotation · three silences became three sentences, and the token meter, the overflow message and the retry gate now share one arithmetic · cross-cutting questions get their own columns

rounds.label: A false unverified on a cooking temperature
rounds.what: Five builders on round 10’s own recorded loss and the defects its new columns surfaced, plus a guard against the harness mistake I made last round.
rounds.findings: My framing of the round’s main task was wrong and a builder proved it. I briefed that the measurement corpus did not span every lookup in a turn; it spans all of them and always did — handed all three lookups the checker returns no finding at all. The defect was WHEN the report was read: lookups two and three were the correction pass’s own, and the app published a verdict older than the evidence. That also meant every rung shared it, so fixing it where I pointed would have repaired one symptom of four. Two other builders refused what they were asked: one declined to enable audit exports everywhere, showing the audit reaches one of twenty statement classes and would make the bench measure an app configured unlike the shipped one, and built a record from already-public APIs instead — settleable statements 9 → 55, runs where nothing was settleable 31/36 → 6, with no file under src/ touched. The other proved the obvious harness guard would have PASSED the sweep it exists to stop, because round 10’s checkouts predate any manifest, and read the measurement vocabulary structurally out of each harness’s source instead — finding a fourth instrumentation field my own hand-written lists had been omitting.
rounds.verdict: Round 11: task — round-11 build 2 · round-10 build 0 · 16 ties. self-consistency and record-consistency both 0 · 0 · 18. The narrowest result the bench has produced, and the honest one: sixteen tasks tied, and on several of them the critics said outright that the behaviour under test was never exercised.
rounds.gap: V1 is recorded twice and the difference matters. As reported it took both cross-cutting columns for this build; but the same critic tied V1’s task column because the entire delta was one space character the model typed — one arm wrote "165 °F", the other "165°F", and the backing checker matches literally. Applied uniformly, the protocol’s own rule makes V1 a tie in all three columns, which is how the round is scored here. Both cross-cutting columns therefore came back 0-0-18, and that is either two clean builds or two columns with nothing to bite on. The critics also found four defects both builds share: a backing checker that over-warns on a space and under-warns on a wrong table row; an unbacked-figures line silently capped at five while its sibling line discloses truncation; "The runtime reported:" left as a label introducing nothing in the collapsed view; and a reply denying tool calls the app is displaying directly above it, which no checking pass looks at.
rounds.fix: The grounding report is graded after the pass that changes the record, so no verdict outlives its evidence · the budget keys on what a pass returned rather than on the clock · a cancelled plan says whose decision it was, and a stalled stream names the party that has not answered · the record block makes 55 of the screen’s statements settleable and names five classes no artifact can settle · a stale harness is refused before the app launches, and both arms’ harness provenance is asserted identical at staging

rounds.label: The checker never reads what the reply says about the app
rounds.what: A reply saying "I did not call any search or reference lookup tools" sits directly above three green-ticked reference_lookup blocks, in both builds, and no checking pass looks at it — the grounding ladder checks a reply’s claims about the world and never its claims about the application. Behind it: a backing checker that flags a correctly-sourced temperature over one space character; an unbacked-figures count silently capped at five; round 10’s own "the reply ran to its end — it was simply empty" printed directly above the refusal it quotes; and round 11’s own "not even the reply headers have come back", which a critic could not settle and which may assert more about the wire than the app can see.
rounds.findings: The first round where both sweeps returned 18/18 VALID with no re-runs, after five that each needed two or three. Two builders again refused the brief. One was asked to flag a reply that names the wrong table row and argued the case back from absence: passage [5] begins mid-row with "ths |", so the app cannot tell which row a value came from and a wrong-row warning would be a guess wearing a certainty. It shipped the narrower true thing — a value-and-dimension match that no longer breaks over the space in "165 °F". The other, asked to make the reply-about-the-app check symmetric, shipped only the denial direction and wrote down why the mirror is not the mirror: a fabricated call inflates authority and the reader can check it against the tool blocks on screen, where a denied call tells the reader those blocks are meaningless and nothing on screen settles that. It also named three neighbouring claims it will not touch, because no artifact here can settle them.
rounds.verdict: Round 12: task — round-12 build 4 · round-11 build 0 · 14 ties. self-consistency 1 · 0 · 17. record-consistency 2 · 0 · 16. The four task wins land exactly on the four behaviours the round changed — two failure banners that now describe what the server actually did, and two plan headers that stop reporting in-flight progress once a plan is over — found by critics who never saw the changelog. Two verdicts were overruled after reporting, in opposite directions, and both by experiment rather than argument.
rounds.gap: The round’s only result against the new build did not survive checking, and neither did one of its wins. TH1 was awarded for a screen reconciling "3 calls accounted for, 1 ran" — but `overstatedToolCounts` is byte-identical in both arms, and the other run simply never over-claimed, so the win was a shared check firing on one side’s tokens. V3 was scored against the new build for a coverage line reading "1 of the 4 measurements" where the critic counted six — but running both arms’ `measurementsIn` over the exact reply bytes returns the same four spans in each, and `quantityCoverage` is byte-identical too, so the app’s 4 matches the app’s own scan. Both became ties. What the second one left behind is real: "~876 drops per day" is a quantity the scan has no unit for, so a line that says "in this reply" counted less than the reply contains. Two more shared defects: the plan header’s "N/N steps done" is the only line visible without interacting and the one number no artifact can settle, because the audit records tools and never steps; and the ledger line miscounts the session variables printed directly beneath it, in both arms, by exactly one, twice. Fourteen ties also mean fourteen tasks that mostly did not exercise what they test — the post-answer wait never happened, the layout probe’s reply side was never echoed, both quotation checks found both replies accurate.
rounds.fix: A measurement is its value and dimension, not the way a passage spelled it · the reply’s account of the application is checked in the denial direction, against the tool blocks printed above it · a failure banner says what the server did rather than what it did not send · a plan that is over stops reporting how far through it is · a cross-cutting column declares what stands behind its verdicts, so silence stops reading as agreement · the ignore rule matches the symlink as well as the directory

rounds.label: Six defects both builds shared, and three briefs the builders proved wrong
rounds.what: Round 12 tied 14 of 18 tasks, and a same-generation tie is where the SHARED defects live — so this round is built entirely out of them. A reply that invents the retrieval whose true account the app printed directly above it (3 record contradictions per run, both arms, the round’s highest contested count). A ledger line that miscounts the session variables listed a few lines beneath it. “Checking stopped at its 60s limit” beside “114.1s checking”. A coverage line claiming “in this reply” over a scan with no unit for “876 drops per day”. Fetch internals reaching the reader past the boundary built to stop them. And the plan header’s “3/3 steps done” — the most prominent claim in plan mode and the one thing the hash-chained audit beside it cannot corroborate, because it records tools and never steps.
rounds.findings: Three of the six briefs I wrote were wrong and the builders proved it from artifacts rather than deferring. I said the runtime string was probably bypassing the failure boundary; it was not — the abort is caught by type and the raw quote is deliberate, and the real fault was that one surface renders a `detail` with no sentence near it, so OPENING the disclosure told a reader less than the line above it. I said the ledger was probably a fencepost; it was not — the absent name sorted second of four, which no off-by-one produces, and the count was correct for a list one turn old, so the label was lying about WHEN, not about how many. I asked whether the 60s budget was enforced; the answer was four lines above the banner in the same message — a deep_research campaign dispatched inside the revision pass ran 93s, because `budget.signal` aborts model streams and nothing reaches `executeTool`. Two builders also refused part of their brief with measurements: widening the measurement scan returns 578 spans over the shipped packs, headed by `529 plans` and `31 March`, and no noun list separates those from `876 drops` — and because `MEASUREMENT_UNITS` is single-sourced and inverted feeds the rung that decides which numbers may support a price, widening it would have moved money verdicts as a side effect. The other split the plan-header complaint in two: UNCORROBORATED is about who is watching and nothing local-first can change it; UNRECORDED was wide open, and a three-step plan that called no tools had been leaving a log in which nothing happened between question and answer.
rounds.verdict: Round 13: task — round-13 build 5 · round-12 build 0 · 13 ties. self-consistency 2 · 0 · 16. record-consistency 2 · 0 · 16. All five task wins trace to a specific change this round, found by critics who never saw the changelog. Three verdicts were overruled after reporting, in both directions, and both corrections fell to the same test: whether the winning behaviour is code the two arms share.
rounds.gap: The round’s only result against the new build did not survive that test, and neither did one of its wins. TTU3 was scored against this build because one arm spent 47.3s checking on FEWER tokens than the arm that spent 0s, and printed "✎ Revised: 1 unsupported item was sent back … the re-check faults none of them" on the same screen as "nothing could be checked against anything" — a real and damning contradiction, but every string in it exists in both arms, and round 13’s budget change moves the origin EARLIER, leaving a pass less time rather than more. TH1 was awarded to this build for a tool-disclosure warning whose producing function is byte-identical across the arms and which fired in 1 of 36 runs. Both became ties. What the round leaves standing is larger than what it fixed: the two context figures on every screen never agree, and the rail figure is byte-identical between arms even when one retrieved eleven passages to the other’s five, so it does not move with the conversation at all; the app prints five passages with relevance scores and then lets the reply say it called no lookup; a checking pass can bill 47 seconds and report clearing a claim on a screen that says nothing was checkable; wrong arithmetic ships unflagged on a prompt that asked for it to be checked; and the HTTP 500 handler still advises the reader how to fix a 403.
rounds.fix: A plan’s step boundaries are written into the hash-chained audit, so the header’s fraction has a witness — and the header is counted from a ledger rather than asserted, with the log deliberately NOT carrying the sentence · a disclosure says what the app read the runtime’s words to mean, glossing the class rather than the string · the coverage line names whose reading its denominator is, and discloses the quantities its vocabulary cannot read at all · the ledger line says it describes the moment the turn began · the checking limit says it bounds what starts, not what finishes, and names the overrun · a reply that misdescribes the retrieval printed above it is checked against the pack, passage count and relevance figures the app already holds

evals.sweeps valid without a re-run: 1 of 2 arms (arm B needed two, both CDP timeouts)

rounds.label: The runtime alone: one tree, Electron 31 against Electron 44

pair.B: the same v2.2.0 tree on Electron 44 (the v2.3 runtime)

rounds.what: v2.3 changes the runtime and nothing else — Electron 31 (Chromium 126, Node 20) to Electron 44 (Chromium 152, Node 24) — and the strategy that scheduled it said the release gate is one bench round that ties or better on every task. So this round is the same v2.2.0 code under two runtimes: arms differ only in the Electron binary, every task is expected to tie by construction, and any result is a statement about the runtime or about noise. Both arms swept 18 of 18 VALID on the first pass with no re-runs; the harness needed two fixes before it could run at all on this machine (the per-run profile moved out of ~/Documents, whose folder-privacy gate refuses the re-signed dev binary renames, and the driver stopped assuming Node 20’s WebSocket flag).
rounds.findings: Seventeen ties as reported, and one result against the new runtime that did not survive experiment. VC3’s dark-theme capture on Electron 44 showed three tool-call headers, the selected conversation and the Rollback/Export actions drawn in the light theme’s ink at 1.05:1, 700ms after the switch. Two more captures per arm found nothing — 1 of 3 on 44, 0 of 3 on 31 — and a direct probe froze the same 150ms colour transition on BOTH runtimes: every element with `transition-colors` held the old ink for over three seconds while plain text switched at once, because a transition only advances when the compositor ticks and a covered window gets none. That is the app’s weakness, present since `transition-colors` first went on a button, and it is now fixed: the theme flips with transitions suspended for two frames, pinned by a style check that measures the guarded switch in a real window. Two things about the instrument: with the launcher shim as the entry, the sidebar badge fell back to Electron’s own version, so every screenshot footer read v31.7.7 or v44.1.1 — the blinding held on names and failed on sight; the capture now writes the arm’s package.json beside the shim. And the critic-prompt generator committed in round 9 had been dropped by the round-13 merge along with its documents; rounds 10–13 were judged from briefings not in the repository. Restored, with the counts block folded in, and a transcriber for the task column so the last hand step in judging has an artifact. Machine facts from the same 36 runs, outside any verdict: the user bubble and reply container paint about twice as fast on Electron 44, and on the seven direct-answer tasks the first reply block appears a median 1.3s sooner with the model’s first token arriving at the same time.
rounds.verdict: Round 14: task — Electron 44 0 · Electron 31 0 · 18 ties, after one verdict against the new runtime was overruled by experiment (VC3, recorded). self-consistency 0 · 0 · 18, contested 4/18. record-consistency 0 · 0 · 18, contested 3/18. The gate the strategy set — ties or better on every task — is met, and the round’s one finding was a defect both runtimes share, fixed before the release.
rounds.gap: The two cross-cutting columns were contested on 4 and 3 of 18 tasks: a same-code pair puts almost nothing in play, which is what a runtime round should look like and is also why it cannot say much beyond ‘nothing broke’. The critics’ biggest-remaining-gap lines name what both builds still do wrong and none of it is new: V1’s ‘3 to 4 days’ lines are ham rows in a chicken question and neither screen says so; TTU2’s sandbox printed ‘Sum = 824693’ under a reply stating 149326778 and the checker called it clean; TTU3 told the reader ‘no source is reachable’ with an installed library never consulted; PT1 keeps every executed call two disclosures deep. Those are round 15’s material, not this round’s.
rounds.fix: App: a theme switch suspends colour transitions for two frames (App.tsx, index.css) · style check: a transition-colors element is measured across a guarded switch in a real window, and what an unguarded switch reads is reported · harness: per-run profile under the OS temp dir; WebSocket flag probed; arm package.json written beside the shim so the version badge names the arm; make-critic-prompts.mjs restored with the counts block; critic-verdicts.mjs transcribes the task column through the withheld key
